lesson.title: From Reflex to Reach: How Infants' Bodies and Brains Take Shape
lesson.summary: In the first two years, infants move from a set of built-in reflexes to purposeful, coordinated action, following a predictable sequence even though the exact timing of each milestone varies widely from child to child.
lesson.body:
Newborns arrive with a set of automatic, unlearned reflexes that helped their ancestors survive. The rooting reflex turns a baby's head toward a touch on the cheek, helping them find a nipple; the sucking reflex lets them feed as soon as something touches the roof of the mouth; the palmar grasp reflex closes an infant's fingers tightly around an object placed in the palm; and the Moro, or startle, reflex causes the arms to fling outward and then draw in when a baby feels like they are falling. Most of these reflexes fade within the first several months as the nervous system that was built during the prenatal period matures and voluntary control takes over.

Motor development after birth generally follows two organizing principles. The cephalocaudal principle describes growth and control proceeding from the head downward, which is why infants can control their eyes and head well before they can control their legs. The proximodistal principle describes growth and control proceeding from the center of the body outward, which is why infants gain control of their trunk and arms before they gain fine control of their fingers.

Within that framework, most infants follow a broadly predictable sequence: rolling over, sitting up without support, crawling, pulling up to stand, and eventually walking independently, often somewhere between about nine and fifteen months. These ages are useful as general guides, but the normal range is wide, and a single child being a few months ahead or behind an average is not, on its own, a sign of a problem.

Underneath these visible milestones, the brain is changing dramatically. Infants are born with far more neural connections than they will keep, and the first years of life involve both an explosive growth of new synapses and a gradual pruning away of connections that go unused, shaped in part by the infant's actual experiences. This is one of the clearest illustrations of nature and nurture working together: the basic sequence of development is guided by a genetic plan, but adequate nutrition, stimulation, and interaction with caregivers matter for how well that plan gets carried out.

This period of rapid physical and neural change sets the stage for the next major transition covered in this unit: the biological and brain changes of adolescence.
